tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, indefinitely** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Timeout → killed. Set `persistent: true` for session-length watches (PR monitoring, log tails) — the monitor runs until you call TaskStop or the session ends. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms, max 3600000ms. Ignored when persistent is true.

persistent.description: Run for the lifetime of the session (no timeout). Use for session-length watches like PR monitoring or log tails. Stop with TaskStop.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

entries.name: TaskCreate
entries.description:
Use this tool to create a structured task list for your current coding session. This helps you track progress, organize complex tasks, and demonstrate thoroughness to the user.
It also helps the user understand the progress of the task and overall progress of their requests.

## When to Use This Tool

Use this tool proactively in these scenarios:

- Complex multi-step tasks - When a task requires 3 or more distinct steps or actions
- Non-trivial and complex tasks - Tasks that require careful planning or multiple operations
- Plan mode - When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work
- User explicitly requests todo list - When the user directly asks you to use the todo list
- User provides multiple tasks - When users provide a list of things to be done (numbered or comma-separated)
- After receiving new instructions - Immediately capture user requirements as tasks
- When you start working on a task - Mark it as in_progress BEFORE beginning work
- After completing a task - Mark it as completed and add any new follow-up tasks discovered during implementation

## When NOT to Use This Tool

Skip using this tool when:
- There is only a single, straightforward task
- The task is trivial and tracking it provides no organizational benefit
- The task can be completed in less than 3 trivial steps
- The task is purely conversational or informational

NOTE that you should not use this tool if there is only one trivial task to do. In this case you are better off just doing the task directly.

## Task Fields

- **subject**: A brief, actionable title in imperative form (e.g., "Fix authentication bug in login flow")
- **description**: What needs to be done
- **activeForm** (optional): Present continuous form shown in the spinner when the task is in_progress (e.g., "Fixing authentication bug"). If omitted, the spinner shows the subject instead.

All tasks are created with status `pending`.

## Tips

- Create tasks with clear, specific subjects that describe the outcome
- After creating tasks, use TaskUpdate to set up dependencies (blocks/blockedBy) if needed
- Check TaskList first to avoid creating duplicate tasks

subject.description: A brief title for the task

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

metadata.description: Arbitrary metadata to attach to the task

entries.name: TaskList
entries.description:
Use this tool to list all tasks in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

- To see what tasks are available to work on (status: 'pending', no owner, not blocked)
- To check overall progress on the project
- To find tasks that are blocked and need dependencies resolved
- After completing a task, to check for newly unblocked work or claim the next available task
- **Prefer working on tasks in ID order** (lowest ID first) when multiple tasks are available, as earlier tasks often set up context for later ones

## Output

Returns a summary of each task:
- **id**: Task identifier (use with TaskGet, TaskUpdate)
- **subject**: Brief description of the task
- **status**: 'pending', 'in_progress', or 'completed'
- **owner**: Agent ID if assigned, empty if available
- **blockedBy**: List of open task IDs that must be resolved first (tasks with blockedBy cannot be claimed until dependencies resolve)

Use TaskGet with a specific task ID to view full details including description and comments.

entries.name: TaskStop
entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

entries.name: TaskUpdate
entries.description:
Use this tool to update a task in the task list.

## When to Use This Tool

**Mark tasks as resolved:**
- When you have completed the work described in a task
- When a task is no longer needed or has been superseded
- IMPORTANT: Always mark your assigned tasks as resolved when you finish them
- After resolving, call TaskList to find your next task

- ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it
- If you encounter errors, blockers, or cannot finish, keep the task as in_progress
- When blocked, create a new task describing what needs to be resolved
- Never mark a task as completed if:
  - Tests are failing
  - Implementation is partial
  - You encountered unresolved errors
  - You couldn't find necessary files or dependencies

**Delete tasks:**
- When a task is no longer relevant or was created in error
- Setting status to `deleted` permanently removes the task

**Update task details:**
- When requirements change or become clearer
- When establishing dependencies between tasks

## Fields You Can Update

- **status**: The task status (see Status Workflow below)
- **subject**: Change the task title (imperative form, e.g., "Run tests")
- **description**: Change the task description
- **activeForm**: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")
- **owner**: Change the task owner (agent name)
- **metadata**: Merge metadata keys into the task (set a key to null to delete it)
- **addBlocks**: Mark tasks that cannot start until this one completes
- **addBlockedBy**: Mark tasks that must complete before this one can start

## Status Workflow

Status progresses: `pending` → `in_progress` → `completed`

Use `deleted` to permanently remove a task.

## Staleness

Make sure to read a task's latest state using `TaskGet` before updating it.

## Examples

Mark task as in progress when starting work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "in_progress"}
```

Mark task as completed after finishing work:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "completed"}
```

Delete a task:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "status": "deleted"}
```

Claim a task by setting owner:
```json
{"taskId": "1", "owner": "my-name"}
```

Set up task dependencies:
```json
{"taskId": "2", "addBlockedBy": ["1"]}
```

taskId.description: The ID of the task to update

activeForm.description: Present continuous form shown in spinner when in_progress (e.g., "Running tests")

"""Paired bootstrap: is model A really better than model B on the same examples?

Resamples example ids with replacement and reports the mean difference (A minus B) in CRPS and
median error with a 95% interval. An interval that excludes zero is a difference the test set
supports; one that straddles zero is not. Cancelled examples are excluded, as in the metrics.

    python trip/bootstrap.py --a "blend=out/trip/eval_step5000/blend_test.npz" \
        --b "xgboost=out/trip/baselines_5000/xgboost_test.npz"
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import metrics

RESAMPLES = 2000


def load(spec: str) -> tuple[str, pd.DataFrame, np.ndarray]:
    """Name, example ids with their row numbers, and quantiles from a ``name=path.npz`` argument."""
    name, path = spec.split("=", 1)
    with np.load(path) as data:
        frame = pd.DataFrame({"example_id": data["example_id"]})
        quantiles = data["quantiles"]
    return name, frame.assign(row=np.arange(len(frame))), quantiles


def main() -> None:
    """Print the bootstrap intervals of A minus B."""
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--a", required=True, help="name=path.npz of the candidate")
    parser.add_argument("--b", required=True, help="name=path.npz of the reference")
    parser.add_argument("--examples", default="data/trip/examples.parquet")
    parser.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    name_a, ids_a, q_a = load(args.a)
    name_b, ids_b, q_b = load(args.b)
    shared = ids_a.merge(ids_b, on="example_id", suffixes=("_a", "_b"))
    examples = pd.read_parquet(args.examples, columns=["example_id", "target_minutes", "cancelled"])
    shared = shared.merge(examples, on="example_id")
    shared = shared[~shared["cancelled"]]
    y = shared["target_minutes"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
    qa, qb = q_a[shared["row_a"].to_numpy()], q_b[shared["row_b"].to_numpy()]

    diffs = {
        "crps": metrics.crps_from_quantiles(y, qa) - metrics.crps_from_quantiles(y, qb),
        "mae_median": np.abs(y - qa[:, metrics.MEDIAN]) - np.abs(y - qb[:, metrics.MEDIAN]),
    }
    rng = np.random.default_rng(args.seed)
    draws = rng.integers(0, len(y), size=(RESAMPLES, len(y)))
    print(f"{name_a} minus {name_b} on {len(y)} shared examples that ran ({RESAMPLES} resamples):")
    for metric, d in diffs.items():
        means = d[draws].mean(axis=1)
        low, high = np.percentile(means, [2.5, 97.5])
        verdict = "better" if high < 0 else "worse" if low > 0 else "no clear difference"
        print(f"  {metric}: {d.mean():+.4f} (95% interval {low:+.4f} to {high:+.4f}) -> {name_a} {verdict}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.content:
"""Post-hoc improvements fitted on validation only, then scored on test.

1. Recalibrate the TSLM's P(cancelled) with Platt scaling: sigmoid(a * logit(p) + b).
2. Blend TSLM and XGBoost: average their quantile functions with weight w, and their
   P(late) and P(cancelled) with the same kind of weight, each chosen by validation score.

    python trip/combine.py --run out/trip/eval_step5000
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import metrics

COLUMNS = ["example_id", "split", "target_minutes", "cancelled", "lead_minutes", "cls", "pre_departure"]
WEIGHTS = np.round(np.arange(0.0, 1.01, 0.05), 2)
EPS = 1e-4


def load(path: Path) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
    """Saved predictions without the (large) full distributions."""
    with np.load(path) as data:

1	"""Post-hoc improvements fitted on validation only, then scored on test.
2	
3	1. Recalibrate the TSLM's P(cancelled) with Platt scaling: sigmoid(a * logit(p) + b).
4	2. Blend TSLM and XGBoost: average their quantile functions with weight w, and their
5	   P(late) and P(cancelled) with the same kind of weight, each chosen by validation score.
6	3. The same blend with one quantile weight per lead-time bucket: the TSLM is strongest close to
7	   arrival and XGBoost further out, so the weight follows the lead time.
8	
9	    python trip/combine.py --run out/trip/eval_step5000
10	"""
11	
12	from __future__ import annotations
13	
14	import argparse
15	import json
16	from pathlib import Path
17	
18	import numpy as np
19	import pandas as pd
20	
21	import metrics
22	
23	COLUMNS = ["example_id", "split", "target_minutes", "cancelled", "lead_minutes", "cls", "pre_departure"]
24	WEIGHTS = np.round(np.arange(0.0, 1.01, 0.05), 2)
25	EPS = 1e-4
26	
27	
28	def load(path: Path) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
29	    """Saved predictions without the (large) full distributions."""
30	    with np.load(path) as data:
31	        return {key: data[key] for key in data.files if key != "probs"}
32	
33	
34	def aligned(pred: dict[str, np.ndarray], ids: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]:
35	    """Arrays reordered to the given example ids."""
36	    order = pd.Series(np.arange(len(pred["example_id"])), index=pred["example_id"]).loc[ids].to_numpy()
37	    return {key: value[order] for key, value in pred.items() if key != "example_id"}
38	
39	
40	def log_loss(p: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> float:
41	    """Binary log loss with clipping."""
42	    p = np.clip(p, EPS, 1 - EPS)
43	    return float(-(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)).mean())
44	
45	
46	def platt(p: np.ndarray, a: float, b: float) -> np.ndarray:
47	    """sigmoid(a * logit(p) + b)."""
48	    p = np.clip(p, EPS, 1 - EPS)
49	    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(a * np.log(p / (1 - p)) + b)))
50	
51	
52	def fit_platt(p: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray) -> tuple[float, float]:
53	    """Grid search for the Platt parameters with the lowest log loss."""
54	    grid = [(a, b) for a in np.arange(0.25, 3.01, 0.05) for b in np.arange(-3.0, 3.01, 0.1)]
55	    return min(grid, key=lambda ab: log_loss(platt(p, *ab), y))
56	
57	
58	def split_data(run: Path, baselines: Path, examples: pd.DataFrame, split: str):
59	    """TSLM and XGBoost predictions on the examples both scored, with their rows."""
60	    tslm = load(run / f"tslm_{split}.npz")
61	    xgb = load(baselines / f"xgboost_{split}.npz")
62	    ids = np.array(sorted(set(tslm["example_id"].tolist()) & set(xgb["example_id"].tolist())))
63	    frame = examples.set_index("example_id").loc[ids].reset_index()
64	    return aligned(tslm, ids), aligned(xgb, ids), frame
65	
66	
67	def blend(tslm: dict, xgb: dict, w: float | np.ndarray, wc: float, cancel: np.ndarray) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
68	    """Quantile average with weight w on the TSLM (a scalar or one weight per example);
69	    P(cancelled) average with weight wc."""
70	    w = np.broadcast_to(np.asarray(w, dtype=np.float64), (len(cancel),))
71	    q = np.sort(w[:, None] * tslm["quantiles"] + (1 - w[:, None]) * xgb["quantiles"], axis=1)
72	    p_late = w * tslm["p_late"] + (1 - w) * xgb["p_late"]
73	    p_cancel = wc * cancel + (1 - wc) * xgb["p_cancel"]
74	    return q, p_late, p_cancel
75	
76	
77	def lead_weights(frame: pd.DataFrame, weights: dict[str, float]) -> np.ndarray:
78	    """One TSLM weight per example, looked up by its lead-time bucket."""
79	    bucket = pd.cut(frame["lead_minutes"], metrics.LEAD_BINS, labels=metrics.LEAD_LABELS)
80	    return bucket.astype(str).map(weights).to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
81	
82	
83	MIN_BUCKET = 100
84	
85	
86	def main() -> None:
87	    """Fit on validation, report test, save the blended predictions."""
88	    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
89	    parser.add_argument("--run", required=True, help="directory with tslm_validation.npz and tslm_test.npz")
90	    parser.add_argument("--baselines", default="out/trip/baselines_5000")
91	    parser.add_argument("--examples", default="data/trip/examples.parquet")
92	    args = parser.parse_args()
93	
94	    run, baselines = Path(args.run), Path(args.baselines)
95	    examples = pd.read_parquet(args.examples, columns=COLUMNS)
96	    v_tslm, v_xgb, v_frame = split_data(run, baselines, examples, "validation")
97	    v_runs = ~v_frame["cancelled"].to_numpy(dtype=bool)
98	    v_y = np.nan_to_num(v_frame["target_minutes"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64))
99	    v_cancel = v_frame["cancelled"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
100	
101	    a, b = fit_platt(v_tslm["p_cancel"], v_cancel)
102	    v_cal = platt(v_tslm["p_cancel"], a, b)
103	
104	    def val_crps(w: float, mask: np.ndarray = v_runs) -> float:
105	        q = np.sort(w * v_tslm["quantiles"] + (1 - w) * v_xgb["quantiles"], axis=1)
106	        return float(metrics.crps_from_quantiles(v_y[mask], q[mask]).mean())
107	
108	    w = min(WEIGHTS, key=val_crps)
109	    v_bucket = pd.cut(v_frame["lead_minutes"], metrics.LEAD_BINS, labels=metrics.LEAD_LABELS)
110	    by_lead: dict[str, float] = {}
111	    for label in metrics.LEAD_LABELS:
112	        mask = (v_bucket == label).to_numpy() & v_runs
113	        # Small buckets keep the global weight rather than a noisy one of their own.
114	        by_lead[label] = float(min(WEIGHTS, key=lambda k: val_crps(k, mask))) if mask.sum() >= MIN_BUCKET else float(w)
115	    wc = min(WEIGHTS, key=lambda c: log_loss(c * v_cal + (1 - c) * v_xgb["p_cancel"], v_cancel))
116	    fitted = {"platt_a": round(float(a), 3), "platt_b": round(float(b), 3), "quantile_weight_tslm": float(w),
117	              "cancel_weight_tslm": float(wc), "quantile_weight_tslm_by_lead": by_lead,
118	              "validation_crps_by_weight": {float(k): round(val_crps(k), 4) for k in WEIGHTS}}
119	    print("fitted on validation:", {k: v for k, v in fitted.items() if k != "validation_crps_by_weight"})
120	
121	    t_tslm, t_xgb, t_frame = split_data(run, baselines, examples, "test")
122	    t_cal = platt(t_tslm["p_cancel"], a, b)
123	    q, p_late, p_cancel = blend(t_tslm, t_xgb, w, wc, t_cal)
124	    q_lead, p_late_lead, _ = blend(t_tslm, t_xgb, lead_weights(t_frame, by_lead), wc, t_cal)
125	    results = {
126	        "xgboost": metrics.evaluate(t_frame, t_xgb["quantiles"], t_xgb["p_cancel"], t_xgb["p_late"]),
127	        "tslm": metrics.evaluate(t_frame, t_tslm["quantiles"], t_tslm["p_cancel"], t_tslm["p_late"]),
128	        "tslm, cancel recalibrated": metrics.evaluate(t_frame, t_tslm["quantiles"], t_cal, t_tslm["p_late"]),
129	        f"blend (w={w}, cancel w={wc})": metrics.evaluate(t_frame, q, p_cancel, p_late),
130	        "blend by lead": metrics.evaluate(t_frame, q_lead, p_cancel, p_late_lead),
131	    }
132	    np.savez_compressed(run / "blend_test.npz", example_id=t_frame["example_id"].to_numpy(), quantiles=q,
133	                        p_cancel=p_cancel, p_late=p_late)
134	    np.savez_compressed(run / "blend_lead_test.npz", example_id=t_frame["example_id"].to_numpy(), quantiles=q_lead,
135	                        p_cancel=p_cancel, p_late=p_late_lead)

content.content:
### Results so far

Learning curve of the main run (soft targets plus CRPS), 300 validation examples:

| Model | Median error | CRPS | 10 to 90% coverage |
|---|---|---|---|
| XGBoost | 2.023 | 1.631 | 0.862 |
| Step 1,000 | 2.100 | 1.701 | 0.948 |
| Step 2,000 | 2.163 | 1.722 | 0.938 |
| Step 4,000 | 2.059 | 1.671 | 0.952 |

Test, the same 5,000 seeded examples for every model:

| Model | Steps | Median error | CRPS | 10 to 90% coverage | Brier late | Cancel log loss |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Persistence | | 3.990 | 3.316 | 0.827 | 0.103 | 0.210 |
| Key history | | 5.873 | 4.999 | 0.628 | 0.158 | 0.189 |
| XGBoost | | 3.698 | 2.971 | 0.822 | 0.087 | 0.140 |
| Main (soft targets plus CRPS) | 5,000 | 3.722 | 2.974 | 0.913 | 0.089 | 0.179 |
| Plain cross-entropy | 2,000 | 3.702 | 2.954 | 0.899 | 0.089 | 0.155 |
| `ecg-sp` starting checkpoint | 2,000 | 3.711 | 2.994 | 0.912 | 0.088 | 0.165 |
| Random encoder | 2,000 | 3.727 | 3.006 | 0.912 | 0.089 | 0.166 |
| Blend: 0.6 main quantiles + 0.4 XGBoost | 5,000 | 3.691 | 2.951 | 0.856 | 0.087 | 0.140 |
| Blend: 0.8 plain quantiles + 0.2 XGBoost | 2,000 | 3.687 | 2.943 | 0.835 | 0.088 | 0.140 |

- **No difference is significant yet.** Paired bootstrap on the 4,729 test examples that ran (95%
  intervals of the CRPS difference): main minus XGBoost +0.003 (-0.059 to +0.054); plain minus
  XGBoost -0.018 (-0.080 to +0.034); plain minus main -0.021 (-0.050 to +0.010); plain blend minus
  XGBoost -0.029 (-0.084 to +0.014). The finalists need the full test set.
- **The TSLM is strongest close to arrival.** Within 15 minutes, plain cross-entropy reaches median
  error 1.109 and CRPS 0.898 against XGBoost's 1.222 and 0.983 (1,941 examples, not bootstrapped yet).
  XGBoost stays better 30 to 60 minutes out.
- **Temperature calibration does not help:** the best temperature on validation is exactly 1.0. The
  high coverage is partly an artefact of whole-minute targets scored with inclusive intervals.
- **Platt scaling of P(cancelled)** helps the main model a little (0.179 to 0.170) but not the plain
  model; blending takes P(cancelled) mostly from XGBoost.
- **Free generation works:** 16 of 16 generated answers parse, with a median error of about 2 minutes.

### Pending at the time of writing

- The main configuration at 2,000 steps (the fair reference for the ablations) and the text-only
  baseline (does the time-series encoder beat numbers in the prompt?).
- Plain cross-entropy at 5,000 steps and with doubled learning rates.
- The plain 2,000-step checkpoint on the full 93,738-example test set.
- The main configuration at 12,000 steps, on an H100 and on the devbox, followed by the September
  forward test.

### Still open

- **TimeF export is quadratic in TimeNet's in-memory conversion** (16k records take 57 s; all 298k
  would take hours). Export in chunks.
- **Team backend bug:** injected job files are sent as plain text instead of base64.

- **No difference is significant yet.** Paired bootstrap on the 4,729 test examples that ran (95%

  error 1.109 and CRPS 0.898 against XGBoost's 1.222 and 0.983 (1,941 examples, not bootstrapped yet).
  XGBoost stays better 30 to 60 minutes out.
'''
new = '''| Blend: 0.8 plain quantiles + 0.2 XGBoost | 2,000 | 3.687 | 2.943 | 0.835 | 0.088 | 0.140 |
| Blend by lead time: plain and XGBoost | 2,000 | 3.646 | 2.924 | 0.831 | 0.086 | 0.140 |
| Blend by lead time: main and XGBoost | 5,000 | 3.671 | 2.950 | 0.856 | 0.087 | 0.140 |

- **Single models do not differ significantly.** Paired bootstrap on the 4,729 test examples that
  ran (95% intervals of the CRPS difference): main minus XGBoost +0.003 (-0.059 to +0.054); plain
  minus XGBoost -0.018 (-0.080 to +0.034); plain minus main -0.021 (-0.050 to +0.010); plain global
  blend minus XGBoost -0.029 (-0.084 to +0.014). The finalists need the full test set.
- **The TSLM is significantly better close to arrival, and worse 15 to 30 minutes out.** Bootstrap
  within lead-time buckets, plain cross-entropy minus XGBoost: within 15 minutes (1,927 examples)
  CRPS -0.085 (-0.211 to -0.001) and median error -0.113 (-0.263 to -0.011); 15 to 30 minutes (744)
  CRPS +0.044 (+0.014 to +0.074); 30 to 60 minutes (747) +0.048 (-0.007 to +0.102). The soft-target
  model shows the same shape with smaller margins.
- **A blend with one weight per lead-time bucket beats XGBoost overall.** Fitted on validation, the
  plain model gets weight 0.9 within 15 minutes of arrival and 0.1 to 0.3 further out. On the test
  examples it wins significantly: CRPS -0.047 (-0.101 to -0.013), median error -0.052 (-0.115 to
  -0.012). It also removes the 15 to 30 minute loss (CRPS 1.683 against XGBoost's 1.681). The same
  blend of the soft-target model is not significant (CRPS -0.021, -0.070 to +0.009). This is the
  product story: the TSLM reads the live signal in the last quarter hour, the tabular model carries
  the longer horizons.
'''
assert old in s
s = s.replace(old, new)
p.write_text(s)

ssh devbox 'cd Jonas/db_delay_tslm && .venv/bin/python - <<PY
import pandas as pd
f = pd.read_parquet("data/trip/forward.parquet", columns=["example_id","train_type","train_number","k_station","t0","k_arr_pt","lead_minutes","target_minutes","cancelled","cls","current_delay"])
f = f[(f["t0"] >= "2026-09-12") & (f["lead_minutes"] >= 5) & (f["lead_minutes"] <= 40)]
m = f.merge(f, on="k_station", suffixes=("_a","_b"))
m = m[(m["train_number_a"] != m["train_number_b"])]
gap = (m["k_arr_pt_b"] - m["k_arr_pt_a"]).dt.total_seconds()/60
t0gap = (m["t0_b"] - m["t0_a"]).dt.total_seconds().abs()/60
m = m[(gap >= 6) & (gap <= 20) & (t0gap <= 10)].assign(gap=gap, t0gap=t0gap)
m = m.sort_values(["cls_a","current_delay_a"], ascending=[True, False])
cols = ["example_id_a","train_type_a","train_number_a","example_id_b","train_type_b","train_number_b","k_station","t0_a","t0_b","k_arr_pt_a","k_arr_pt_b","gap","current_delay_a","target_minutes_a","target_minutes_b","cancelled_a","cancelled_b"]
pd.set_option("display.width", 250)
print(len(m)); print(m[cols].head(25).to_string())
PY'

"""Write trip examples as a TimeF dataset: four series, annotations and two tasks per record.

Each record's relative zero is local midnight 30 days before the prediction moment. The daily
history starts there; the two hourly series start 72 hours before the hour of the prediction
moment. The run's delays sit on an ordinal axis, because they follow stops, not a clock.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import sys
import time
from fractions import Fraction
from pathlib import Path
from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset, TimeSeries
from timenet.dataset.axis import OrdinalAxis, RegularAxis
from timenet.types import Annotation, ClassificationTask, DataSource, DatasetMetadata, ScalarPredictionTask, TimeSeriesSpec, ureg

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))

import prompts  # noqa: E402

TZ = ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")
HISTORY_DAYS = 30
SERIES_HOURS = 72
DAY = Fraction(1, 86_400)
HOUR = Fraction(1, 3_600)
CARD = Path(__file__).parent / "timenet_connector" / "dataset.yaml"
SOURCE = DataSource(
    data_source_type="operational-record",
    name="Deutsche Bahn timetable scrape",
    provider="piebro/deutsche-bahn-data",
)
SPECS = {
    "run_departure_delay": TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type="run-departure-delay", name="Departure delay at each stop so far",
                                          unit_value=ureg.minute, data_source=SOURCE),
    "history_daily_median_delay": TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type="history-arrival-delay", name="Daily median arrival delay, last 30 days",
                                                 unit_value=ureg.minute, data_source=SOURCE),
    "station_late_share": TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type="station-late-share", name="Hourly share of late stops at the target station",
                                         unit_value=ureg.dimensionless, data_source=SOURCE),
    "network_late_share": TimeSeriesSpec(spec_type="network-late-share", name="Hourly share of late stops for the train class",
                                         unit_value=ureg.dimensionless, data_source=SOURCE),
}
ANNOTATED = ("split", "cls", "train_type", "train_number", "origin", "dest", "k_station", "hist_level",
             "pre_departure", "lead_minutes", "stops_ahead", "current_delay")


def plain(value):
    """A cell as a plain Python scalar that TimeF annotations accept."""
    if isinstance(value, np.generic):
        value = value.item()
    if isinstance(value, float) and np.isnan(value):
        return None
    return value


def add_example(dataset: TimeFDataset, row: pd.Series) -> None:
    """Append one example as a record with its series, annotations and tasks."""
    rid = f"trip-{int(row['example_id'])}"
    t0 = pd.Timestamp(row["t0"])
    zero = (t0.normalize() - pd.Timedelta(days=HISTORY_DAYS)).to_pydatetime()
    hourly_start = int((t0.floor("h") - pd.Timedelta(hours=SERIES_HOURS) - pd.Timestamp(zero)) / pd.Timedelta(hours=1))
    parts = [
        ("history_daily_median_delay", row["hist_series"], RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(DAY)),
        ("station_late_share", row["station_series"], RegularAxis(period_us=RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(HOUR).period_us,
                                                                  start_index=hourly_start)),
        ("network_late_share", row["network_series"], RegularAxis(period_us=RegularAxis.from_rate_hz(HOUR).period_us,
                                                                  start_index=hourly_start)),
    ]
    run = prompts.as_list(row["run_delays"])
    if run:  # before departure there is no stop yet, so the record has no run series
        parts.insert(0, ("run_departure_delay", run, OrdinalAxis()))
    series = tuple(
        TimeSeries.from_values(np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float32), spec=SPECS[signal], signal=signal,
                               time_axis=axis, source_id=rid, time_series_id=f"{rid}-{signal}")
        for signal, values, axis in parts
    )
    record = dataset.add_record(time_series=series, subject_ids=(prompts.train_label(row),), record_id=rid,
                                start_time=zero.replace(tzinfo=TZ))
    # TimeF rejects an annotation without a value, so fields the scrape lost are left out.
    values = {key: plain(row[key]) for key in ANNOTATED}
    annotations = [Annotation(key=key, value=value, id=f"{rid}-{key}") for key, value in values.items() if value is not None]
    annotations += [
        Annotation(key="prediction_moment", value=t0.isoformat(), id=f"{rid}-t0"),
        Annotation(key="planned_arrival", value=pd.Timestamp(row["k_arr_pt"]).isoformat(), id=f"{rid}-arr"),
    ]
    record.add_annotations(annotations)
    stop = prompts.name(row["k_station"])
    tasks = [ClassificationTask(prompt=f"Will the train be cancelled at {stop}?",
                                target="cancelled" if row["cancelled"] else "runs", target_schema="cancelled|runs",
                                id=f"{rid}-cancelled")]
    if not row["cancelled"]:
        tasks.append(ScalarPredictionTask(prompt=f"How many minutes late will the train arrive at {stop}?",
                                          target=float(row["target_minutes"]), unit="minute",
                                          target_name="arrival_delay_minutes", rationale=prompts.rationale(row),
                                          id=f"{rid}-delay"))
    dataset.add_tasks(record, tasks)


def to_timef(frame: pd.DataFrame, metadata: DatasetMetadata) -> TimeFDataset:
    """Convert a frame of built examples into a TimeF dataset."""
    dataset = TimeFDataset(metadata=metadata)
    for i in range(len(frame)):
        add_example(dataset, frame.iloc[i])
    return dataset


def verify(path: Path) -> dict:
    """Open a written version, run TimeNet's integrity check, and count what it holds."""
    from timenet.reader.reader import TimeFReader
    from timenet.registry.version import DatasetVersion

    with TimeFReader(DatasetVersion.open_local(path)) as reader:
        reader.verify()
        tasks = reader.tasks() if callable(reader.tasks) else reader.tasks
        records = sum(1 for _ in reader.iter_records())
        metadata = reader.metadata() if callable(reader.metadata) else reader.metadata
    return {"dataset_id": metadata.dataset_id, "version": str(metadata.dataset_version),
            "records": records, "tasks": len(tasks)}


def main() -> None:
    """Export built examples to TimeF and read the result back."""
    from timenet.writer.writer import TimeFWriter

    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--examples", default="data/trip/examples.parquet")
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="out/trip/timef")
    parser.add_argument("--split", choices=["train", "validation", "test"])
    parser.add_argument("--limit", type=int)
    parser.add_argument("--verify-only", help="a written version directory to check instead of exporting")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    if args.verify_only:
        print("verified:", verify(Path(args.verify_only)))
        return

    frame = pd.read_parquet(args.examples)
    if args.split:
        frame = frame[frame["split"] == args.split]
    if args.limit:
        frame = frame.sample(n=min(args.limit, len(frame)), random_state=0)
    started = time.time()
    dataset = to_timef(frame.reset_index(drop=True), DatasetMetadata.from_yaml(CARD))
    converted = time.time() - started
    dataset.derive_schema()
    root = Path(args.out)
    with TimeFWriter(root, dataset) as writer:
        writer.write()
    path = root / dataset.metadata.dataset_id / str(dataset.metadata.dataset_version)
    print(f"converted {len(frame)} examples in {converted:.1f}s, wrote {path} in {time.time() - started - converted:.1f}s")
    print(f"in memory: {len(dataset.records)} records, {len(dataset.tasks)} tasks")
    print("verified:", verify(path))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""TimeNet connector for ``error404/db-trip-delay``: German rail trip delay from the public DB scrape.

``download`` fetches the processed monthly parquet files from Hugging Face into the cache,
skipping files already there. ``convert`` runs the trip example builder over them and writes
one TimeF record per example. Connectors take no constructor arguments, so the months and the
example scale come from environment variables.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os
import sys
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd
from timenet.connectors import BaseConnector
from timenet.dataset import TimeFDataset

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import build  # noqa: E402
import timef_export  # noqa: E402

URL = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data/resolve/main/monthly_processed_data/data-{}.parquet"
DEFAULT_MONTHS = "2025-11,2025-12,2026-01,2026-02,2026-03,2026-04,2026-05,2026-06,2026-07,2026-08"


class DbTripDelayConnector(BaseConnector[Path]):
    """Monthly scrape files in, one record per (run, target stop, prediction moment) out."""

    def download(self, cache_dir: Path) -> list[Path]:
        """Fetch each month once; a partial download is written aside and renamed when complete.

        Args:
            cache_dir: Where the monthly files live.

        Returns:
            The local paths, in month order.
        """
        months = os.environ.get("DB_TRIP_MONTHS", DEFAULT_MONTHS).split(",")
        paths = []
        for month in months:
            path = Path(cache_dir) / f"data-{month}.parquet"
            if not path.exists():
                part = path.with_suffix(".part")
                urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL.format(month), part)
                part.rename(path)
            paths.append(path)
        return paths

    def convert(self, raw_refs: list[Path]) -> TimeFDataset:
        """Build the examples with :mod:`build` and convert them with :mod:`timef_export`.

        Args:
            raw_refs: Monthly parquet files from :meth:`download`.

        Returns:
            The dataset, one record per example.
        """
        scale = float(os.environ.get("DB_TRIP_SCALE", "1.0"))
        base = build.Config(files=tuple(str(p) for p in raw_refs))
        cfg = build.Config(files=base.files,
                           examples_per_class={k: int(v * scale) for k, v in base.examples_per_class.items()})
        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
            table = build.build(cfg, Path(tmp) / "examples.parquet")
        frame: pd.DataFrame = table.to_pandas()
        return timef_export.to_timef(frame, self.metadata())


CONNECTOR = DbTripDelayConnector

    def set_task_stream(self, task_types: Sequence[type[Task]], source: Callable[[], Iterator[Task]]) -> None:
        """Provide tasks as a re-iterable stream instead of materializing them in the dataset.

        For a dataset with far more tasks than records (many questions over few recordings), holding
        every task in memory is the scaling wall. A streaming connector builds the bounded records and
        registered annotations, then hands the tasks over through ``source``; the writer streams them to
        disk without a list. Streamed tasks are trusted, not validated the way :meth:`add_task` validates
        them: each must already have its ``record_ids`` set and reference only registered annotations and
        existing records. Streamed tasks do not populate ``Record.task_ids``.

        Args:
            task_types: The task classes the stream yields, so :meth:`derive_schema` records them.
                Every yielded task must be one of these types.
            source: A callable returning a fresh iterator over the tasks each time it is called. The
                writer calls it more than once (a peek for id storage, then the write), so it must
                re-read its source rather than exhaust a one-shot generator.

        Raises:
            TimeFValidationError: If tasks were already added with :meth:`add_task`. A dataset either
                streams its tasks or materializes them, never both, or the writer would drop one set.
        """
        if self._tasks:
            raise TimeFValidationError(

def sample(row: pd.Series, text_only: bool = False) -> dict:
    """One OpenTSLM sample, plus the answer prefix used to read out the distribution.

    With ``text_only`` the four series are written into the prompt as numbers and no series
    is passed, which is the baseline without a time-series encoder.
    """
    arrival = pd.Timestamp(row["k_arr_pt"])
    via = [v for v in as_list(row["via"]) if isinstance(v, str) and v]
    stop = name(row["k_station"])
    via_text = f" via {', '.join(via[:5])}{' and further stops' if len(via) > 5 else ''}" if via else ""
    where = (f"It has not departed from {name(row['first_station'])} yet." if row["pre_departure"]
             else f"It has just left {name(row['j_station'])}.")
    pre_prompt = (
        f"You predict how late a German train will arrive, for a traveller. Train {train_label(row)} from "
        f"{name(row['origin'])} to {name(row['dest'])}. {where} Target stop: {stop}{via_text}, planned arrival "
        f"{WEEKDAYS[arrival.weekday()]} {arrival:%H:%M}."
    )
    run = as_list(row["run_delays"])
    raw = [
        ("Departure delay at each stop so far" if run else "No departures yet", run or [0.0], "minutes"),
        (f"Daily median arrival delay at {stop}, last 30 days", row["hist_series"], "minutes"),
        (f"Hourly share of late stops at {stop}, last 72 hours", row["station_series"], "share"),
        (f"Hourly share of late {row['cls']} stops nationwide, last 72 hours", row["network_series"], "share"),
    ]
    if text_only:
        # Baseline: the same numbers written into the prompt, so no time-series encoder is involved.
        lines = [f"{label}, in {'percent' if unit == 'share' else unit}: "
                 f"{as_text(np.asarray(values, dtype=np.float64) * (100 if unit == 'share' else 1))}"
                 for label, values, unit in raw]
        pre_prompt = pre_prompt + "\n" + "\n".join(lines)
        series = []
    else:
        series = [normalised(values, label, unit) for label, values, unit in raw]
    post_prompt = (f"How many minutes late will the train arrive at {stop}? Reason from the data, "
                   f"then answer with whole minutes or {CANCELLED}.\nRationale:")
    reasoning = rationale(row)
    return {
        "pre_prompt": pre_prompt,
        "time_series_text": [text for text, _ in series],
        "time_series": [values for _, values in series],
        "post_prompt": post_prompt,
        "answer": f"{reasoning} Answer: {target_text(row)}",
        "prefix": f"{reasoning} Answer:",
        "example_id": int(row["example_id"]),
    }

content.subject: Probe data semantics across months
content.description: Check schema of Nov 2025 to Aug 2026 files, meaning of time / delay_in_min, run id from `id`, stop numbering.

content.subject: Build trip examples with leakage-safe features
content.description: DuckDB pipeline: runs, sampled (t0 stop, target stop) pairs, 4 series (run so far, fallback-key 30-day history, station 72h, network class 72h), text fields, tabular features, target minutes/cancelled, time split train/val/test. Smoke tests on synthetic data.

content.subject: Implement baselines and shared metrics
content.description: Persistence, key-history, XGBoost quantile + cancel classifier; metrics MAE of median, quantile CRPS, 10-90 coverage, P(late) Brier, cancel log loss, per lead bucket and class.

content.subject: Implement TSLM model, loss and readout
content.description: OpenTSLMSP subclass on unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B + m4-sp checkpoint: right padding, custom loss (CE on rationale, soft CE + CRPS at number token, hurdle cancel step), one-pass distribution readout, tests for token positions.

content.subject: Train and evaluate the TSLM on the devbox
content.description: Smoke train, then full run on the RTX 6000 Ada; evaluate on test with the shared metrics next to baselines; plain-CE ablation if time allows.

content.subject: Update DESIGN.md with implementation decisions and results
content.description: Rationale built from inputs only (never states the minute), loss only at the answer token, deviations found during implementation, results table.

content.subject: Implement connection and journey probability
content.description: P(change works) from arriving and departing delay distributions, planned buffer and minimum transfer time; chained journey success; tests.

content.subject: Export trip examples as a TimeF dataset
content.description: TimeNet connector-style export of examples (four series, minute and cancellation tasks, metadata card) for the bonus points and dataset documentation.

content.subject: Forward test on live September data
content.description: Build examples from the raw September scrape (or Timetables API), predict before arrival, score once arrivals are published.

content.subject: Run ablations and text-only baseline on Nebius H100 jobs
content.description: Four one-GPU H100 jobs (2000 steps each): plain CE, text-only, ecg-sp start, random encoder; results in bucket runs/h100b-*; compare with compare_ablations.sh against baselines and the main run.

content.subject: Probe data semantics across months
content.description: Check schema of Nov 2025 to Aug 2026 files, meaning of time / delay_in_min, run id from `id`, stop numbering.

content.subject: Build trip examples with leakage-safe features
content.description: DuckDB pipeline: runs, sampled (t0 stop, target stop) pairs, 4 series (run so far, fallback-key 30-day history, station 72h, network class 72h), text fields, tabular features, target minutes/cancelled, time split train/val/test. Smoke tests on synthetic data.

content.subject: Implement baselines and shared metrics
content.description: Persistence, key-history, XGBoost quantile + cancel classifier; metrics MAE of median, quantile CRPS, 10-90 coverage, P(late) Brier, cancel log loss, per lead bucket and class.

content.subject: Implement TSLM model, loss and readout
content.description: OpenTSLMSP subclass on unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B + m4-sp checkpoint: right padding, custom loss (CE on rationale, soft CE + CRPS at number token, hurdle cancel step), one-pass distribution readout, tests for token positions.

content.subject: Train and evaluate the TSLM on the devbox
content.description: Smoke train, then full run on the RTX 6000 Ada; evaluate on test with the shared metrics next to baselines; plain-CE ablation if time allows.

content.subject: Update DESIGN.md with implementation decisions and results
content.description: Rationale built from inputs only (never states the minute), loss only at the answer token, deviations found during implementation, results table.

content.subject: Implement connection and journey probability
content.description: P(change works) from arriving and departing delay distributions, planned buffer and minimum transfer time; chained journey success; tests.

content.subject: Export trip examples as a TimeF dataset
content.description: TimeNet connector-style export of examples (four series, minute and cancellation tasks, metadata card) for the bonus points and dataset documentation.

content.subject: Forward test on live September data
content.description: Build examples from the raw September scrape (or Timetables API), predict before arrival, score once arrivals are published.

content.subject: Run ablations and text-only baseline on Nebius H100 jobs
content.description: Four one-GPU H100 jobs (2000 steps each): plain CE, text-only, ecg-sp start, random encoder; results in bucket runs/h100b-*; compare with compare_ablations.sh against baselines and the main run.

"""Write a Nebius job spec for one trip-delay run, always injecting the runner from disk.

A spec copied from an older job carries the runner it was built with, so a change to
run_ablations.sh is silently missing from jobs built that way. This takes an existing spec only
for the parts that do not change (image, platform, bucket volume) and fills in the rest.

    python job_spec.py --template path/to/any-job.json --tag h100-text-plain \
        --custom-args "--loss-mode plain --prompt-mode text --grad-checkpointing" > job.json
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import base64
import json
from pathlib import Path

RUNNER = Path(__file__).with_name("run_ablations.sh")


def main() -> None:
    """Print the spec as JSON."""
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--template", required=True, help="an existing spec: image, platform and volume are kept")
    parser.add_argument("--tag", required=True, help="RUN_TAG; results land under runs/<tag>/ in the bucket")
    parser.add_argument("--name", help="job name; default jonas-<tag>")
    parser.add_argument("--runs", default="custom", help="RUNS selector of run_ablations.sh")
    parser.add_argument("--custom-args", default="", help="train.py arguments for the custom run")

content.content:
- **Read created IDs with `--format jsonpath='{.metadata.id}'`.** Regex over the create output grabs other IDs from the response; every follow-up call then fails with a misleading `NotFound`, which looks like a permission problem.
- **S3 access keys exist only for service accounts** (`nebius iam v2 access-key create --account-service-account-id ... --secret-delivery-mode inline`). The Nebius CLI has no object upload; uploads go through the S3 API (AWS CLI via `uvx --from awscli aws`, endpoint `https://storage.eu-north1.nebius.cloud`).
- **Bucket-only write access:** bucket policy rules take a group, not a service account. Put the service account in a dedicated group and add `{"group_id": ..., "paths": ["*"], "roles": ["storage.editor"]}` to the bucket.
- **Injected job files must be base64** in the jobs API (proto bytes). The team backend sends plain text, so its `submit --script` path is broken; `submit-spec` with pre-encoded content works.
- **Images:** `pytorch/pytorch:2.7.1` has Python 3.11, but `opentslm` needs 3.12; `nvidia/cuda:13.1.1-runtime-ubuntu24.04` plus uv works on L40S (driver 580, CUDA 13.1).
- **Shared project:** teammates may delete jobs they don't recognise; prefix job names with `jonas-`.

Related: [[llama-mirror]].

content.subject: Probe data semantics across months
content.description: Check schema of Nov 2025 to Aug 2026 files, meaning of time / delay_in_min, run id from `id`, stop numbering.

content.subject: Build trip examples with leakage-safe features
content.description: DuckDB pipeline: runs, sampled (t0 stop, target stop) pairs, 4 series (run so far, fallback-key 30-day history, station 72h, network class 72h), text fields, tabular features, target minutes/cancelled, time split train/val/test. Smoke tests on synthetic data.

content.subject: Implement baselines and shared metrics
content.description: Persistence, key-history, XGBoost quantile + cancel classifier; metrics MAE of median, quantile CRPS, 10-90 coverage, P(late) Brier, cancel log loss, per lead bucket and class.

content.subject: Implement TSLM model, loss and readout
content.description: OpenTSLMSP subclass on unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B + m4-sp checkpoint: right padding, custom loss (CE on rationale, soft CE + CRPS at number token, hurdle cancel step), one-pass distribution readout, tests for token positions.

content.subject: Train and evaluate the TSLM on the devbox
content.description: Smoke train, then full run on the RTX 6000 Ada; evaluate on test with the shared metrics next to baselines; plain-CE ablation if time allows.

content.subject: Update DESIGN.md with implementation decisions and results
content.description: Rationale built from inputs only (never states the minute), loss only at the answer token, deviations found during implementation, results table.

content.subject: Implement connection and journey probability
content.description: P(change works) from arriving and departing delay distributions, planned buffer and minimum transfer time; chained journey success; tests.

content.subject: Export trip examples as a TimeF dataset
content.description: TimeNet connector-style export of examples (four series, minute and cancellation tasks, metadata card) for the bonus points and dataset documentation.

content.subject: Forward test on live September data
content.description: Build examples from the raw September scrape (or Timetables API), predict before arrival, score once arrivals are published.

content.subject: Run ablations and text-only baseline on Nebius H100 jobs
content.description: Four one-GPU H100 jobs (2000 steps each): plain CE, text-only, ecg-sp start, random encoder; results in bucket runs/h100b-*; compare with compare_ablations.sh against baselines and the main run.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Move job inputs and results between this machine and the Nebius bucket over the S3 API.
#
#   bash sync_bucket.sh upload <examples.parquet>     package trip/ and upload data and code
#   bash sync_bucket.sh results <run tag> <local dir> download logs and predictions of a run
#   bash sync_bucket.sh ls                            list the bucket
#
# Credentials come from the repo-root .env: NEBIUS_S3_ENDPOINT, NEBIUS_S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID and
# NEBIUS_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY (a service-account access key; only tenant admins can create one).
# The AWS CLI runs through uvx, so nothing is installed globally.
set -euo pipefail

    s3 ls --recursive "s3://$BUCKET/"
    ;;
  cat)
    s3 cp "s3://$BUCKET/${2:?usage: sync_bucket.sh cat <object key>}" -
    ;;
  *)
    sed -n '2,9p' "$0"
    exit 1
    ;;
esac

content.text:
Yes, three things are worth doing now, all off the GPU:

1. **Literature on "LLM reads numbers as text vs. a time-series encoder."** Our strongest finding (text-only beats the encoder) has a known backdrop: LLMTime (Gruver et al. 2023) and "Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?" (Tan et al. 2024). Getting the exact claims and citations lets DESIGN present it as a corroborated result instead of a surprise.
2. **Train-delay prediction literature and typical error numbers**, so we can say where our 3.4 minutes of median error sits, and whether the baselines we beat are the ones the field uses.
3. **Re-checking the challenge PDF's deliverables and judging criteria against what exists**, plus a look at whether our XGBoost baseline is properly tuned (a win over a weak baseline is hollow).

Launching two research agents for 1 and 2; I'll do 3 myself.

input.description: Literature: LLMs vs encoders on time series
input.prompt:
You are doing a focused literature check for a hackathon write-up. Context: we fine-tuned an OpenTSLM-style model (Llama 3.2 3B with a soft-prompt time-series encoder, LoRA) to predict German train arrival delays as a distribution over minutes. Our ablation found that writing the four input series into the prompt as plain numbers (no time-series encoder) beats the same model trained with the time-series encoder at equal steps, and that the starting checkpoint (pretrained encoder vs random) makes no difference. Against a tuned XGBoost with the same features, the LLM wins only within 15 minutes of arrival and a lead-time-dependent blend wins overall.

Find and summarise, with exact citations (authors, year, venue, arXiv id or URL), what the literature says about:
1. LLMs reading numeric time series as text tokens (LLMTime, Gruver et al. 2023; any follow-ups on tokenisation of numbers, Llama 3 digit tokenisation).
2. Whether LLM components help on time-series tasks at all ("Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?", Tan et al. NeurIPS 2024; Time-LLM; any rebuttals or later work up to 2026).
3. The OpenTSLM paper itself (Stanford/ETH, 2025): what it claims about soft-prompt vs flamingo variants, and any ablations comparing text-only inputs.
4. Any work on combining LLM forecasts with gradient boosting or on horizon-dependent ensembling.

Use web search and fetch the papers' abstracts or relevant sections; do not rely on memory alone for numbers or claims. Return a compact report (under 600 words): for each item, the claim in one or two sentences, the citation, and one sentence on how it relates to our finding. Use no em dashes anywhere in the report.

input.description: Literature: train delay prediction
input.prompt:
You are doing a focused literature and landscape check for a hackathon write-up on predicting German (Deutsche Bahn) train arrival delays per stop, at a given prediction moment during the run, as a probability distribution over minutes plus a cancellation probability. Our numbers on a held-out time split (June to August 2026 test, about 94k examples): median absolute error about 3.4 minutes, CRPS about 2.7 minutes, across long-distance, regional and S-Bahn trains, with lead times from minutes to hours before arrival. Baselines: persistence (current delay carried forward), route history, XGBoost quantile regression.

## Literature check: LLM time-series inputs, usefulness, OpenTSLM, ensembling

### 1. LLMs reading numbers as text tokens

**Claim.** LLMTime encodes a series as digit strings and treats forecasting as next-token prediction; GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 then extrapolate zero-shot at a level "comparable to or exceeding" purpose-built models. The paper stresses that "careful tokenization is important for good forecasting with LLMs": GPT-3's BPE chunks "4223563042235630" as [422,35,630], so they insert spaces between digits, whereas "in many new open-source LLMs (e.g. LLaMA), numbers are tokenized into individual digits by default" and spacing hurts LLaMA-2.
**Citation.** Gruver, Finzi, Qiu, Wilson. "Large Language Models Are Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasters." NeurIPS 2023. arXiv:2310.07820.
**Follow-ups.** Singh and Strouse, "Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs," arXiv:2402.14903 (2024): GPT-3.5/4 "have separate tokens for each 1-, 2-, and 3-digit numbers" and right-to-left chunking "leads to largely improved performance". Llama 3 uses the same 0 to 999 chunking (Llama 2 was digit-level), documented in beren.io, "Integer tokenization is now much less insane" (2024). Zhang et al., "From Tokenizer Bias to Backbone Capability: A Controlled Study of LLMs for Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2504.08818 (2025, rev. 2026): learned tokenizer/detokenizer pairs "often overfit to the specific data distribution, thereby masking the intrinsic predictive capability of the LLM backbone."
**Relation.** Our plain-number prompt is the LLMTime recipe applied to Llama 3.2; delay minutes are small integers (mostly under 1000), so each value is one token, which is the regime where text encoding is cheapest and cleanest.

### 2. Do LLM components help at all?

**Claim.** Tan et al. ablate three LLM forecasters and find that "removing the LLM component or replacing it with a basic attention layer does not degrade forecasting performance"; pretrained LLMs "do no better than models trained from scratch" and "do not assist in few-shot settings." Time-LLM (Jin et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.01728) is the opposing claim: reprogrammed frozen LLMs "outperform state-of-the-art, specialized forecasting models" and "excel in both few-shot and zero-shot learning."
**Citation.** Tan, Merrill, Gupta, Althoff, Hartvigsen. "Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?" NeurIPS 2024 (Spotlight). arXiv:2406.16964.
**Rebuttal.** Qiu et al., "Rethinking the Role of LLMs in Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2602.14744 (Feb 2026): on roughly 8 billion observations, "LLM4TS indeed improves forecasting performance," with "pretraining critical under distribution shifts"; prior negative results "stem from limited evaluation settings."
**Relation.** Our "pretrained encoder vs random init makes no difference" mirrors Tan et al.'s from-scratch finding; the added learned modality adapter is exactly the component they show to be dispensable.

### 3. OpenTSLM

**Claim.** Two variants: SoftPrompt (PatchTST-style patch encoder projected into the token stream, LLM tuned with LoRA) and Flamingo (gated cross-attention, frozen backbone). The v1 abstract states Flamingo "matches OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt in performance and outperforms on longer sequences, while maintaining stable memory" (110 GB vs 40 GB on ECG-QA with Llama-3B; v3 reports >180 GB vs up to 60 GB). Text-only baselines write the series as tokens: fine-tuned Llama-3.2-3B gets 60.44 F1 on HAR-CoT vs 65.44 for OpenTSLM, but collapses on Sleep-CoT (5.86 F1) and goes OOM on ECG-QA ("80k tokens"). There is no ablation on encoder initialisation or on removing curriculum stages.
**Citation.** Langer, Kaar, Rosenblattl, Xu, et al. (Stanford, ETH Zurich, UIUC, Google Research). "OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data." arXiv:2510.02410 (Oct 2025, v3 Feb 2026; OpenReview PlYAAdwBy1).
**Relation.** OpenTSLM's advantage over text-only inputs appears only where series are long; our four short series sit in the regime (HAR) where the gap is a few F1 points, which is consistent with plain text winning at equal steps.

### 4. Combining with gradient boosting, horizon-dependent blending

**Claim.** No paper was found blending LLM forecasts with XGBoost by lead time. The closest precedent is the forecast-combination literature: Wang, Hyndman, Li, Kang, "Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review," International Journal of Forecasting 2023, arXiv:2205.04216 (time-varying weights); Cerqueira and Torgo, "Multi-output Ensembles for Multi-step Forecasting," arXiv:2306.14563 (per-horizon vs shared weights on 3,568 series; "as the horizon increases, most approaches struggle to outperform" equal weights); Ray et al., arXiv:2201.12387 (COVID Hub: per-horizon weights help at 1 to 2 weeks, hurt at 3 to 4). Domain baseline: Elliker et al., "RIDE: An Open Dataset and Benchmark for Train Delay Prediction," arXiv:2606.05070 (Belgian network, graph neural nets best, results broken down by horizon).
**Relation.** Our lead-time-dependent blend is a standard horizon-varying combination; the literature warns that per-horizon weights overfit when the calibration set is small, so a smooth weight-vs-lead-time schedule is the defensible choice.

Sources: [arXiv:2310.07820](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07820), [arXiv:2402.14903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14903), [beren.io](https://www.beren.io/2024-05-11-Integer-tokenization-is-now-much-less-insane/), [arXiv:2504.08818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08818), [arXiv:2406.16964](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16964), [arXiv:2310.01728](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01728), [arXiv:2602.14744](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14744), [arXiv:2510.02410](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410), [OpenTSLM GitHub](https://github.com/StanfordBDHG/OpenTSLM), [arXiv:2205.04216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04216), [arXiv:2306.14563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14563), [arXiv:2201.12387](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12387), [arXiv:2606.05070](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05070)</result>
