content.text:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the Artifact tool's description lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

## Literature check: LLM time-series inputs, usefulness, OpenTSLM, ensembling

### 1. LLMs reading numbers as text tokens

**Claim.** LLMTime encodes a series as digit strings and treats forecasting as next-token prediction; GPT-3 and LLaMA-2 then extrapolate zero-shot at a level "comparable to or exceeding" purpose-built models. The paper stresses that "careful tokenization is important for good forecasting with LLMs": GPT-3's BPE chunks "4223563042235630" as [422,35,630], so they insert spaces between digits, whereas "in many new open-source LLMs (e.g. LLaMA), numbers are tokenized into individual digits by default" and spacing hurts LLaMA-2.
**Citation.** Gruver, Finzi, Qiu, Wilson. "Large Language Models Are Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasters." NeurIPS 2023. arXiv:2310.07820.
**Follow-ups.** Singh and Strouse, "Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs," arXiv:2402.14903 (2024): GPT-3.5/4 "have separate tokens for each 1-, 2-, and 3-digit numbers" and right-to-left chunking "leads to largely improved performance". Llama 3 uses the same 0 to 999 chunking (Llama 2 was digit-level), documented in beren.io, "Integer tokenization is now much less insane" (2024). Zhang et al., "From Tokenizer Bias to Backbone Capability: A Controlled Study of LLMs for Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2504.08818 (2025, rev. 2026): learned tokenizer/detokenizer pairs "often overfit to the specific data distribution, thereby masking the intrinsic predictive capability of the LLM backbone."
**Relation.** Our plain-number prompt is the LLMTime recipe applied to Llama 3.2; delay minutes are small integers (mostly under 1000), so each value is one token, which is the regime where text encoding is cheapest and cleanest.

### 2. Do LLM components help at all?

**Claim.** Tan et al. ablate three LLM forecasters and find that "removing the LLM component or replacing it with a basic attention layer does not degrade forecasting performance"; pretrained LLMs "do no better than models trained from scratch" and "do not assist in few-shot settings." Time-LLM (Jin et al., ICLR 2024, arXiv:2310.01728) is the opposing claim: reprogrammed frozen LLMs "outperform state-of-the-art, specialized forecasting models" and "excel in both few-shot and zero-shot learning."
**Citation.** Tan, Merrill, Gupta, Althoff, Hartvigsen. "Are Language Models Actually Useful for Time Series Forecasting?" NeurIPS 2024 (Spotlight). arXiv:2406.16964.
**Rebuttal.** Qiu et al., "Rethinking the Role of LLMs in Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2602.14744 (Feb 2026): on roughly 8 billion observations, "LLM4TS indeed improves forecasting performance," with "pretraining critical under distribution shifts"; prior negative results "stem from limited evaluation settings."
**Relation.** Our "pretrained encoder vs random init makes no difference" mirrors Tan et al.'s from-scratch finding; the added learned modality adapter is exactly the component they show to be dispensable.

### 3. OpenTSLM

**Claim.** Two variants: SoftPrompt (PatchTST-style patch encoder projected into the token stream, LLM tuned with LoRA) and Flamingo (gated cross-attention, frozen backbone). The v1 abstract states Flamingo "matches OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt in performance and outperforms on longer sequences, while maintaining stable memory" (110 GB vs 40 GB on ECG-QA with Llama-3B; v3 reports >180 GB vs up to 60 GB). Text-only baselines write the series as tokens: fine-tuned Llama-3.2-3B gets 60.44 F1 on HAR-CoT vs 65.44 for OpenTSLM, but collapses on Sleep-CoT (5.86 F1) and goes OOM on ECG-QA ("80k tokens"). There is no ablation on encoder initialisation or on removing curriculum stages.
**Citation.** Langer, Kaar, Rosenblattl, Xu, et al. (Stanford, ETH Zurich, UIUC, Google Research). "OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data." arXiv:2510.02410 (Oct 2025, v3 Feb 2026; OpenReview PlYAAdwBy1).
**Relation.** OpenTSLM's advantage over text-only inputs appears only where series are long; our four short series sit in the regime (HAR) where the gap is a few F1 points, which is consistent with plain text winning at equal steps.

### 4. Combining with gradient boosting, horizon-dependent blending

**Claim.** No paper was found blending LLM forecasts with XGBoost by lead time. The closest precedent is the forecast-combination literature: Wang, Hyndman, Li, Kang, "Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review," International Journal of Forecasting 2023, arXiv:2205.04216 (time-varying weights); Cerqueira and Torgo, "Multi-output Ensembles for Multi-step Forecasting," arXiv:2306.14563 (per-horizon vs shared weights on 3,568 series; "as the horizon increases, most approaches struggle to outperform" equal weights); Ray et al., arXiv:2201.12387 (COVID Hub: per-horizon weights help at 1 to 2 weeks, hurt at 3 to 4). Domain baseline: Elliker et al., "RIDE: An Open Dataset and Benchmark for Train Delay Prediction," arXiv:2606.05070 (Belgian network, graph neural nets best, results broken down by horizon).
**Relation.** Our lead-time-dependent blend is a standard horizon-varying combination; the literature warns that per-horizon weights overfit when the calibration set is small, so a smooth weight-vs-lead-time schedule is the defensible choice.

Sources: [arXiv:2310.07820](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.07820), [arXiv:2402.14903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.14903), [beren.io](https://www.beren.io/2024-05-11-Integer-tokenization-is-now-much-less-insane/), [arXiv:2504.08818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.08818), [arXiv:2406.16964](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.16964), [arXiv:2310.01728](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01728), [arXiv:2602.14744](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.14744), [arXiv:2510.02410](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.02410), [OpenTSLM GitHub](https://github.com/StanfordBDHG/OpenTSLM), [arXiv:2205.04216](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.04216), [arXiv:2306.14563](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.14563), [arXiv:2201.12387](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12387), [arXiv:2606.05070](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05070)</result>

**Follow-ups.** Singh and Strouse, "Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs," arXiv:2402.14903 (2024): GPT-3.5/4 "have separate tokens for each 1-, 2-, and 3-digit numbers" and right-to-left chunking "leads to largely improved performance". Llama 3 uses the same 0 to 999 chunking (Llama 2 was digit-level), documented in beren.io, "Integer tokenization is now much less insane" (2024). Zhang et al., "From Tokenizer Bias to Backbone Capability: A Controlled Study of LLMs for Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2504.08818 (2025, rev. 2026): learned tokenizer/detokenizer pairs "often overfit to the specific data distribution, thereby masking the intrinsic predictive capability of the LLM backbone."

### 2. Do LLM components help at all?

**Claim.** Tan et al. ablate three LLM forecasters and find that "removing the LLM component or replacing it with a basic attention layer does not degrade forecasting performance"; pretrained LLMs "do no better than models trained from scratch" and "do not assist in few-shot settings." **Rebuttal.** Qiu et al., "Rethinking the Role of LLMs in Time Series Forecasting," arXiv:2602.14744 (Feb 2026): on roughly 8 billion observations, "LLM4TS indeed improves forecasting performance," with "pretraining critical under distribution shifts"; prior negative results "stem from limited evaluation settings."
**Relation.** Our "pretrained encoder vs random init makes no difference" mirrors Tan et al.'s from-scratch finding; the added learned modality adapter is exactly the component they show to be dispensable.

### 3. OpenTSLM

**Claim.** Two variants: SoftPrompt (PatchTST-style patch encoder projected into the token stream, LLM tuned with LoRA) and Flamingo (gated cross-attention, frozen backbone). The v1 abstract states Flamingo "matches OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt in performance and outperforms on longer sequences, while maintaining stable memory" (110 GB vs 40 GB on ECG-QA with Llama-3B; v3 reports >180 GB vs up to 60 GB). Text-only baselines write the series as tokens: fine-tuned Llama-3.2-3B gets 60.44 F1 on HAR-CoT vs 65.44 for OpenTSLM, but collapses on Sleep-CoT (5.86 F1) and goes OOM on ECG-QA ("80k tokens"). There is no ablation on encoder initialisation or on removing curriculum stages.
**Citation.** Langer, Kaar, Rosenblattl, Xu, et al. (Stanford, ETH Zurich, UIUC, Google Research). "OpenTSLM: Time-Series Language Models for Reasoning over Multivariate Medical Text- and Time-Series Data." arXiv:2510.02410 (Oct 2025, v3 Feb 2026; OpenReview PlYAAdwBy1).
**Relation.** OpenTSLM's advantage over text-only inputs appears only where series are long; our four short series sit in the regime (HAR) where the gap is a few F1 points, which is consistent with plain text winning at equal steps.

### 4. Combining with gradient boosting, horizon-dependent blending

**Claim.** No paper was found blending LLM forecasts with XGBoost by lead time. ## Literature and landscape check: DB per-stop delay prediction

### 1. Academic work

1. **Nair, Hoang, Laumanns, Chen, Cogill, Szabó, Walter (2019), Transportation Research Part C 104.** Ensemble (context-aware random forest, kernel regression, simulation) on Deutsche Bahn's full network (about 25,000 trains/day). Baseline is the published timetable. Reports 25% better "correctness" (share within 1 min) and 50% lower RMSE; RMSE grows from about 110 s (0 to 10 min ahead) to 400 to 500 s (180+ min ahead). [ADS record](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019TRPC..104..196N/abstract)

2. **Spanninger, Trivella, Büchel, Corman (2022), J. Rail Transport Planning & Management 22.** Review of 71 papers. Reported real-time MAEs: Kecman & Goverde 2015 (NS) about 40 s beyond 20 min; Oneto et al. 2018 (Italian RFI, extreme learning machines) 1.5 to 2.5 min for 1 to 5 stations ahead; Corman & Kecman 2018 (Bayesian networks, Sweden) 30 to 100 s over 0 to 60 min. Most data-driven work is deterministic; probabilistic outputs are rare. [PDF](https://ris.utwente.nl/ws/files/278073033/1_s2.0_S2210970622000166_main.pdf)

3. **Elliker, Le Bail, Mantoux, Read, Vanier (2026), RIDE benchmark, arXiv 2606.05070.** Belgian network, 94.5M events, temporal split (train 2023 to 2024, test 2025), predict next 15 events (about 40 min). Test MAE: persistence 1.61 min, XGBoost 1.28, LSTM 1.24, GNN 1.23; at 45+ min all models degrade to 4 to 5 min MAE. The paper calls persistence "surprisingly strong" and "difficult to beat by a large margin". [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.05070)

4. **Sobrie, Verschelde, Hennebel, Roets (2023), EJOR 310.** LSTM encoder-decoder for real-time delay prediction at Infrabel; beats the rule-based operational forecaster by 18% (23% in complex situations). [ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0377221723002631)

5. **Spanninger, Wiedemann, Corman (2024), Transportation Research Part C.** Uncertainty-aware neural nets (test-time dropout, loss attenuation) on Swiss data; predictability decays exponentially with horizon and depends on train category (regional vs intercity). Closest published analogue to a distributional target. [ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0968090X24000846)

6. **Kampere & Alsahag (2025), arXiv 2507.11776.** XGBoost with network centrality features on NS data; reports limited performance under non-simultaneous (forward-in-time) testing. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11776)

### 2. Open-source DB projects

7. **Bahn-Vorhersage (Döllmann et al.), GitLab and Augsburg OPUS dataset paper (2025).** Polls the DB Timetable API for all stations since September 2021 (about 700 GB, ODbL). Predicts transfer-success probabilities from train type, time, route so far and forecast time; no published MAE, only the claim that its punctuality statistics match official DB figures. [OPUS](https://opus.bibliothek.uni-augsburg.de/opus4/frontdoor/index/index/year/2026/docId/127213), [GitLab](https://gitlab.com/bahnvorhersage/bahnvorhersage)

8. **piebro/deutsche-bahn-data (Hugging Face, CC BY 4.0).** IRIS timetable scrapes, roughly 226M rows, top 100 stations from 2024-07, all stations since 2025-11, with `delay_in_min` and cancellation flags. No accompanying model or accuracy. [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data)

### 3. DB's own forecasting

9. **DB "RI-Prognose" (since 2018) and heise (2025).** ML trained on historical patterns plus live network messages, GPS positions, dispatcher inputs; about 150M forecasts/day refreshed every two minutes. DB reports 74% accuracy for stop cancellations and platform changes (target 80% by 2027) and aims to announce stop cancellations 60 min ahead. No delay MAE is published. [DB](https://www.deutschebahn.com/de/kuenstlicheintelligenz-6898594), [heise](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Forecasting-machine-How-AI-is-set-to-improve-rail-travel-information-10343595.html)

### 4. Reference statistics

10. Official punctuality (under 6 min): long-distance 60.1% in 2025 (62.5% in 2024), regional 88.7%, all passenger trains 88.0%; H1 2026 long-distance 58.7% with 8% of long-distance trains fully or partly cancelled (ministry answer to a parliamentary inquiry, August 2026). Cancellations are excluded from the punctuality figure. [eisenbahn.de](https://eisenbahn.de/geramond-vgb/jahresbilanz-2025-puenktlichkeit-der-deutschen-bahn-sinkt-weiter_17653), [schiene.de](https://www.schiene.de/news-12105/Etwa-jeder-zwoelfte-DB-Fernzug-ganz-oder-teilweise-ausgefallen.html)

### Where our numbers sit

Our 25% of stops at least 6 min late is a plausible blend of about 40% for long-distance and about 11% for regional stops; 5% cancelled is consistent with 8% partial-or-full long-distance cancellations diluted by regional and S-Bahn traffic. On error, the field is not directly comparable: published MAEs of 0.5 to 2.5 min come from short horizons (next station, under 40 min) on denser, more punctual networks, and RIDE shows 4 to 5 min MAE once horizons exceed 45 min. Our median AE of 3.4 min and CRPS of 2.7 min over horizons up to hours on a German summer with 60% long-distance punctuality is therefore in the expected band, but should be reported per horizon bucket to be credible. The baseline the field expects is persistence (last known delay carried forward), with XGBoost as the standard learned reference; RIDE makes explicit that beating persistence by a wide margin is hard, so stating our gain over it per horizon is the key comparison. Probabilistic per-stop output with CRPS is rare in this literature (Spanninger 2024, Corman & Kecman 2018 are the nearest), which is a legitimate novelty claim for the write-up.</result>

Temporal AI Challenge · error404 · DB trip delay

Trip Delay Run Ledger

Every model we trained tonight, what it scored, and what is still on the GPUs. Times are Zurich; the hackathon ends Saturday 12:00.

As ofSat 13 Sep, 00:28

The idea in one breath

A traveller shares a trip. For the train they are on and the stop they are heading to, we predict a distribution over arrival delay in whole minutes, plus the chance the train is cancelled, and turn that into "about +1 min, likely 0 to 5, 92% on time" and "96% chance of making your change". The model is OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B with LoRA: the language model reads the live situation (delay at each stop so far, route history, station and network lateness) and answers with one minute token per outcome, which we read out as a full probability distribution in one forward pass.

DuckDB over the monthly parquet files. Every input is computed strictly before the prediction moment; station and network hours end before the hour it falls in. Hash-seeded sampling per train class.

As ofSat 13 Sep, 00:28

## Literature and landscape check: DB per-stop delay prediction

### 1. Academic work

1. **Nair, Hoang, Laumanns, Chen, Cogill, Szabó, Walter (2019), Transportation Research Part C 104.** Ensemble (context-aware random forest, kernel regression, simulation) on Deutsche Bahn's full network (about 25,000 trains/day). Baseline is the published timetable. Reports 25% better "correctness" (share within 1 min) and 50% lower RMSE; RMSE grows from about 110 s (0 to 10 min ahead) to 400 to 500 s (180+ min ahead). [ADS record](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019TRPC..104..196N/abstract)

2. **Spanninger, Trivella, Büchel, Corman (2022), J. Rail Transport Planning & Management 22.** Review of 71 papers. Reported real-time MAEs: Kecman & Goverde 2015 (NS) about 40 s beyond 20 min; Oneto et al. 2018 (Italian RFI, extreme learning machines) 1.5 to 2.5 min for 1 to 5 stations ahead; Corman & Kecman 2018 (Bayesian networks, Sweden) 30 to 100 s over 0 to 60 min. [DB](https://www.deutschebahn.com/de/kuenstlicheintelligenz-6898594), [heise](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Forecasting-machine-How-AI-is-set-to-improve-rail-travel-information-10343595.html)

10. Official punctuality (under 6 min): long-distance 60.1% in 2025 (62.5% in 2024), regional 88.7%, all passenger trains 88.0%; H1 2026 long-distance 58.7% with 8% of long-distance trains fully or partly cancelled (ministry answer to a parliamentary inquiry, August 2026). Cancellations are excluded from the punctuality figure. [eisenbahn.de](https://eisenbahn.de/geramond-vgb/jahresbilanz-2025-puenktlichkeit-der-deutschen-bahn-sinkt-weiter_17653), [schiene.de](https://www.schiene.de/news-12105/Etwa-jeder-zwoelfte-DB-Fernzug-ganz-oder-teilweise-ausgefallen.html)

### Where our numbers sit

Our 25% of stops at least 6 min late is a plausible blend of about 40% for long-distance and about 11% for regional stops; 5% cancelled is consistent with 8% partial-or-full long-distance cancellations diluted by regional and S-Bahn traffic. On error, the field is not directly comparable: published MAEs of 0.5 to 2.5 min come from short horizons (next station, under 40 min) on denser, more punctual networks, and RIDE shows 4 to 5 min MAE once horizons exceed 45 min. Our median AE of 3.4 min and CRPS of 2.7 min over horizons up to hours on a German summer with 60% long-distance punctuality is therefore in the expected band, but should be reported per horizon bucket to be credible. The baseline the field expects is persistence (last known delay carried forward), with XGBoost as the standard learned reference; RIDE makes explicit that beating persistence by a wide margin is hard, so stating our gain over it per horizon is the key comparison. Probabilistic per-stop output with CRPS is rare in this literature (Spanninger 2024, Corman & Kecman 2018 are the nearest), which is a legitimate novelty claim for the write-up.</result>

input.content:
Temporal AI Challenge · error404 · DB trip delay

Trip Delay Run Ledger

What we are building, every model we trained tonight, how well each one did, and what is still running. Times are Zurich; the hackathon ends Saturday 12:00.

As ofSat 13 Sep, 00:35

What we are building

A traveller shares a trip: the train they are on and the stop they want to reach. We answer two questions at that moment: how late will the train arrive there, and will it be cancelled. The answer is not a single number but a range with probabilities, which we turn into plain sentences: "about +1 min, likely 0 to 5, 92% chance you are on time" and, for a connection, "96% chance of making your change".

The model is a time-series language model: Llama 3.2 (3 billion parameters) from the OpenTSLM project, lightly fine-tuned by us. It gets the live situation as input (how late the train was at each stop so far, how this route usually does, how the station and the whole network are doing right now) and writes an answer in minutes. Because every minute from 0 to 999 is a single word to this model, we can read off the probability of every possible delay in one go, which is what gives us the range.

298,430training and test examples, each one a real train at a real moment with a real target stop
Nov 25 to Aug 26public DB timetable data. Trained on data up to 1 May, tuned on May, tested on June to August
21,982extra September examples, scraped after the training data was frozen: a true "future" test
2 answersdelay range in minutes, plus the chance of cancellation

The pieces everything that exists besides the model

Data preparation

Turns raw monthly timetable files into examples. Every input is something that was known before the prediction moment, so the model can never peek at the answer.

done

Yardstick models

Three simpler models to compare against. The important one is XGBoost, a classic and very strong machine-learning method (gradient-boosted decision trees) that gets exactly the same information as our model. If we cannot beat it, the language model brings nothing.

done

Scoring

Every model is scored on the same test trips with the same script: how far off the "most likely" delay was, how good the range was, and how well the cancellation chance was calibrated. Split out by train type and by how far ahead the prediction was made.

done

Luck check

A statistical test that tells whether a difference between two models is real or could be a fluke of which trips landed in the test set. Explained under the chart below.

done tonight

Blending

Instead of picking one model, mix the language model's forecast with XGBoost's. Tonight we learned that the best mix depends on how close the train is to the stop.

done tonight

TimeNet connector and dataset

The challenge asks for data in TimeNet's format. Our connector downloads, builds and converts the data; the finished dataset (298,430 records) passed TimeNet's own check. A speed bug in the conversion was found and fixed tonight.

done tonight

Demo

A command-line tool takes a trained model and real trips and prints the traveller view, including the chance of making a connection. Tested on two ICE trains meeting at Göttingen this morning. There is no web interface yet.

CLI only

Compute

One GPU box of our own for the long run (about 1 second per training step) and rented H100 GPUs on Nebius for everything else (0.3 seconds per step). Six H100 jobs tonight.

running

Documentation

DESIGN.md holds every decision (sections 1 to 15), tonight's results (16) and how they relate to published research (17). All committed and pushed.

current

Every run we did scored on the same 5,000 test trips

How to read the numbers. Both scores are in minutes and lower is better. Median error: how far the model's single best guess was from the real delay, on average. CRPS: how good the whole predicted range was; it rewards putting probability where the truth landed and punishes ranges that are too wide or off-centre. "Val" is the May data we used for tuning; "Test" is June to August, which no model saw during training. The differences between rows look small because most trains are nearly on time; the hard cases are where models differ.

A "run" is one training of the model with one set of choices. Steps are training iterations; more steps means the model saw more examples. An ablation is an experiment that changes exactly one ingredient to find out whether that ingredient matters.

Side note on the long run on our own box: on a small check set of 300 May trips it keeps improving with training (median error 2.100 at step 1,000, 2.059 at 4,000, 1.983 at 8,000; XGBoost gets 2.023 on those 300). So the long runs are worth finishing.

How much better or worse than XGBoost CRPS difference, 5,000 test trips

How to read this chart. Each bar is one model compared with XGBoost. The middle line is "exactly as good as XGBoost". A bar pointing left means the model's forecast range is better (lower CRPS); a bar pointing right means worse. The number on the right is the difference in minutes of CRPS.

The thin line through each bar is the luck check. We re-scored both models on 2,000 random re-draws of the test trips; the line spans the range of results those re-draws gave. If the whole line sits left of the middle, the model won on practically every re-draw, so the win is real. If the line crosses the middle, the two models could just as well be equal and the difference may be chance. Green bars are wins that passed this check. Grey bars either failed it or were not checked.

Green: better than XGBoost, and the luck check says it is real. Grey: the difference could be chance, or we did not run the check for this row. Thin line: the range of outcomes across the 2,000 re-draws (a 95% interval).

Why the single models are grey and the blends green: on 5,000 trips a difference of 0.03 to 0.05 minutes is inside the noise. The blends have a bigger margin, and on the full 93,738 trips even the smaller margins become clear (see below).

What we know for sure each of these passed the luck check

Mixing our model with XGBoost by lead time beats XGBoost on all test trips

Checked on 88,479 trips that actually ran: the mix is better by 0.028 minutes of CRPS (the plausible range is 0.019 to 0.039, all on the winning side) and by 0.035 minutes of median error. The mixing ratio was chosen on May data only and then applied blind to June to August.

−0.028CRPS vs XGBoost, full test

On its own, our model wins the last quarter hour before arrival

For predictions made within 15 minutes of the planned arrival (36,556 trips), its best guess is off by 0.991 minutes on average against XGBoost's 1.072, and its range is better by 0.055 CRPS. Further out, XGBoost is better (by 0.076 CRPS beyond 30 minutes). That is exactly why the mix uses our model close to arrival and XGBoost further away.

0.99 vs 1.07minutes off, last 15 min

The special time-series encoder is not pulling its weight

Writing the numbers into the prompt as plain text beats feeding them through OpenTSLM's time-series encoder, with the same training otherwise (0.057 CRPS better, range 0.026 to 0.090). Whether the encoder starts pretrained or from scratch makes no difference. Published research says the same: language models read short number sequences well as text, and the encoder mainly pays off for very long signals such as ECGs.

−0.057text vs encoder, CRPS

The simpler training signal works better

Rewarding only the exact right minute ("plain loss") gives better ranges than our original signal that also rewarded near misses: 0.041 CRPS better (range 0.011 to 0.069). Training longer keeps helping. Doubling the learning rate changes nothing.

−0.041plain vs original, CRPS

The probabilities are already well calibrated

We tried two standard ways of re-scaling the model's confidence after training; the best setting was "leave it as is". The cancellation chance in the mix comes mostly from XGBoost, which is better at it. Every free-text answer the model wrote could be parsed into a number.

Glossary

XGBoost
A widely used, very strong machine-learning method based on decision trees. It is our yardstick: it gets the same inputs as our model, so any gain over it is due to the language model, not to better data.
Median error
Take the model's single most likely delay, compare it with what really happened, average the difference in minutes over all trips that ran. Lower is better.
CRPS
A score for a whole forecast range rather than a single guess. It is low when the range is narrow and centred on what happened, high when it is wide or off. Also in minutes; lower is better.
Lead time
How many minutes before the planned arrival the prediction was made. Predicting 5 minutes ahead is easy; 2 hours ahead is hard. Our buckets: up to 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 120, more than 120 minutes.

A traveller shares a trip. For the train they are on and the stop they are heading to, we predict a distribution over arrival delay in whole minutes, plus the chance the train is cancelled, and turn that into "about +1 min, likely 0 to 5, 92% on time" and "96% chance of making your change". The model is OpenTSLM on Llama 3.2 3B with LoRA: the language model reads the live situation (delay at each stop so far, route history, station and network lateness) and answers with one minute token per outcome, which we read out as a full probability distribution in one forward pass.

+

A traveller shares a trip: the train they are on and the stop they want to reach. We answer two questions at that moment: how late will the train arrive there, and will it be cancelled. The answer is not a single number but a range with probabilities, which we turn into plain sentences: "about +1 min, likely 0 to 5, 92% chance you are on time" and, for a connection, "96% chance of making your change".

+

The model is a time-series language model: Llama 3.2 (3 billion parameters) from the OpenTSLM project, lightly fine-tuned by us. It gets the live situation as input (how late the train was at each stop so far, how this route usually does, how the station and the whole network are doing right now) and writes an answer in minutes. Because every minute from 0 to 999 is a single word to this model, we can read off the probability of every possible delay in one go, which is what gives us the range.

How to read the numbers. Both scores are in minutes and lower is better. Median error: how far the model's single best guess was from the real delay, on average. CRPS: how good the whole predicted range was; it rewards putting probability where the truth landed and punishes ranges that are too wide or off-centre. "Val" is the May data we used for tuning; "Test" is June to August, which no model saw during training. The differences between rows look small because most trains are nearly on time; the hard cases are where models differ.

+

A "run" is one training of the model with one set of choices. Steps are training iterations; more steps means the model saw more examples. An ablation is an experiment that changes exactly one ingredient to find out whether that ingredient matters.

How to read this chart. Each bar is one model compared with XGBoost. The middle line is "exactly as good as XGBoost". A bar pointing left means the model's forecast range is better (lower CRPS); a bar pointing right means worse. The number on the right is the difference in minutes of CRPS.

+

The thin line through each bar is the luck check. We re-scored both models on 2,000 random re-draws of the test trips; the line spans the range of results those re-draws gave. If the whole line sits left of the middle, the model won on practically every re-draw, so the win is real. If the line crosses the middle, the two models could just as well be equal and the difference may be chance. Green bars are wins that passed this check. Grey bars either failed it or were not checked.

The lead-aware blend beats XGBoost on the full test set

88,479 running examples: CRPS −0.028 (−0.039 to −0.019), median error −0.035 (−0.047 to −0.024). The weights fitted on May put 0.95 on the TSLM within 15 minutes of arrival and 0.1 to 0.3 further out.

The TSLM alone wins the last quarter hour

Within 15 minutes of planned arrival (36,556 examples): median error 0.991 vs 1.072 minutes, CRPS −0.055 (−0.081 to −0.034). Beyond 30 minutes XGBoost is better by +0.076 CRPS, so the TSLM alone is slightly worse overall (+0.015).

The time-series encoder is not earning its place

Numbers written into the prompt beat the same recipe with the encoder at 2,000 steps: CRPS −0.057 (−0.090 to −0.026). Pretrained vs random encoder makes no difference. This matches LLMTime (Gruver et al. 2023) and Tan et al. (NeurIPS 2024); OpenTSLM's own text-only baseline only falls behind on long series.

−0.057text only vs reference

Plain cross-entropy beats the soft-target loss

CRPS −0.041 (−0.069 to −0.011) at equal steps; median error unchanged. Doubling the learning rates does nothing. More steps keep helping (5k vs 2k: −0.031, interval just crossing zero).

−0.041plain vs soft, CRPS

-

Temperature and Platt scaling barely matter

The best temperature on validation is exactly 1.0. Platt scaling of P(cancelled) helps the soft model a little; the blend takes P(cancelled) mostly from XGBoost. Every generated free-text answer parsed.

T = 1.0calibration

+

Mixing our model with XGBoost by lead time beats XGBoost on all test trips

Checked on 88,479 trips that actually ran: the mix is better by 0.028 minutes of CRPS (the plausible range is 0.019 to 0.039, all on the winning side) and by 0.035 minutes of median error. The mixing ratio was chosen on May data only and then applied blind to June to August.

−0.028CRPS vs XGBoost, full test

+

On its own, our model wins the last quarter hour before arrival

For predictions made within 15 minutes of the planned arrival (36,556 trips), its best guess is off by 0.991 minutes on average against XGBoost's 1.072, and its range is better by 0.055 CRPS. Further out, XGBoost is better (by 0.076 CRPS beyond 30 minutes). That is exactly why the mix uses our model close to arrival and XGBoost further away.

0.99 vs 1.07minutes off, last 15 min

+

The special time-series encoder is not pulling its weight

Writing the numbers into the prompt as plain text beats feeding them through OpenTSLM's time-series encoder, with the same training otherwise (0.057 CRPS better, range 0.026 to 0.090). Whether the encoder starts pretrained or from scratch makes no difference. Published research says the same: language models read short number sequences well as text, and the encoder mainly pays off for very long signals such as ECGs.

−0.057text vs encoder, CRPS

+

The simpler training signal works better

Rewarding only the exact right minute ("plain loss") gives better ranges than our original signal that also rewarded near misses: 0.041 CRPS better (range 0.011 to 0.069). Training longer keeps helping. Doubling the learning rate changes nothing.

−0.041plain vs original, CRPS

+

The probabilities are already well calibrated

We tried two standard ways of re-scaling the model's confidence after training; the best setting was "leave it as is". The cancellation chance in the mix comes mostly from XGBoost, which is better at it. Every free-text answer the model wrote could be parsed into a number.

-    <dt>Lead time</dt><dd>Minutes between the prediction moment and the planned arrival at the target stop. Buckets: ≤ 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 120, more.</dd>

-    <dt>Soft targets plus CRPS</dt><dd>The original loss: the minute distribution is trained towards a bump around the true minute plus a CRPS term. "Plain" is ordinary cross-entropy on the one true token.</dd>

-    <dt>Paired bootstrap</dt><dd>Resample the same test examples 2,000 times and recompute the difference between two models each time; an interval that excludes zero is a difference the test set supports.</dd>
-    <dt>Lead-time blend</dt><dd>Average the TSLM and XGBoost quantile functions with a weight that depends on the lead-time bucket, fitted on validation only, applied to test.</dd>

+    <dt>XGBoost</dt><dd>A widely used, very strong machine-learning method based on decision trees. It is our yardstick: it gets the same inputs as our model, so any gain over it is due to the language model, not to better data.</dd>
+    <dt>Median error</dt><dd>Take the model's single most likely delay, compare it with what really happened, average the difference in minutes over all trips that ran. Lower is better.</dd>

+    <dt>CRPS</dt><dd>A score for a whole forecast range rather than a single guess. It is low when the range is narrow and centred on what happened, high when it is wide or off. Also in minutes; lower is better.</dd>

+    <dt>Lead time</dt><dd>How many minutes before the planned arrival the prediction was made. Predicting 5 minutes ahead is easy; 2 hours ahead is hard. Our buckets: up to 15, 15 to 30, 30 to 60, 60 to 120, more than 120 minutes.</dd>

+    <dt>Luck check (paired bootstrap)</dt><dd>Randomly re-draw the test trips 2,000 times, score both models on each re-draw, and look at the range of differences. If the range does not include zero, one model wins consistently and the difference is not a fluke of the sample.</dd>

+    <dt>Blend</dt><dd>An average of two models' forecasts. "80% ours, 20% XGBoost" means the forecast range is four parts ours and one part XGBoost. The lead-time blend uses a different ratio depending on how far the train is from the stop; the ratios were chosen on May data and then frozen.</dd>

+    <dt>Plain loss vs original loss</dt><dd>The training signal. The original also gave partial credit for near misses (predicting 3 when the truth was 4) and for a well-shaped range; the plain version only rewards the exact minute. Simpler turned out better.</dd>

+    <dt>Text only vs encoder</dt><dd>Two ways of giving the model its input series. "Encoder" is OpenTSLM's dedicated component that converts a number series into something the language model can read; "text only" simply writes the numbers into the prompt.</dd>
+    <dt>Steps</dt><dd>Training iterations. Each step shows the model a batch of 8 examples; 12,000 steps is roughly half a pass over the training data.</dd>

message.content: What is the lead-time blend? And what are the "numbers for this better / worse charts saying? And I see a lot of text-only. What is not-text-only. Does the time-series data actually help?

content.text:
Three plain answers.

**1. The lead-time blend.** "Lead time" is how many minutes before the planned arrival we make the prediction. The blend is an average of our model's forecast and XGBoost's, and the mixing ratio depends on that lead time. Concretely, with the plain-5k model: a train 8 minutes from the stop gets 90% our model, 10% XGBoost; a train 90 minutes away gets 35% ours, 65% XGBoost; between 30 and 60 minutes it is 100% XGBoost. We use it because the two are good at different things: our model reads the live signal of the last few stops best, XGBoost is better at the long-range averages. The ratios were picked on May data and frozen before scoring the test.

**2. The numbers in the chart.** They are differences in CRPS, in minutes. "−0.064" means that model's average CRPS is 0.064 minutes lower than XGBoost's: 2.907 instead of 2.971, roughly 2% better. Honest reading: on average over all trips the gains are small. What makes it interesting is *where* they come from: within 15 minutes of arrival our model's typical error is 0.99 minutes against XGBoost's 1.07, about 8% better, and that is exactly the moment a traveller is deciding whether to run for a connection.

**3. Text-only vs. the rest, and does the time-series data help.** Two different questions hide in there.

- *Not text-only* is the standard OpenTSLM setup: the four input series (delay at each stop so far, this route's daily history, hourly lateness at the station, hourly lateness on the network) go through a dedicated **time-series encoder**, a small neural network that converts a series into internal tokens the language model can attend to but never sees as digits. *Text-only* skips that component and writes the same series into the prompt as numbers.
- **Does the time-series data help? Yes, a lot.** Every model on the page uses it, including XGBoost. The one that does not, "persistence" (just carry the current delay forward), scores 3.316 CRPS against about 2.94 for the models that read the series. The live series are what make the forecasts good.
- **Does the encoder help? No, not on our data.** Feeding the same numbers as text beats feeding them through the encoder (0.057 CRPS better at equal training), and an untrained encoder does as well as a pretrained one. Published work agrees for short series; the encoder pays off on long signals like ECGs, and our series have at most 72 points. The run finishing around 00:55 ("text and encoder + plain loss") answers the last version of the question: does adding the encoder *on top of* the text help at all.

For the pitch the honest framing is: it is still a language model reasoning over temporal signals and explaining itself; the specific encoder component did not earn its place here, and we can show why.

Three good questions; the third one deserves a real check rather than an answer from memory, so I'm reading the loss code now. First the quick two:

**Persistence is missing from the chart** because it is off the scale: +0.345 CRPS worse than XGBoost, five times the width of the chart's right side. I'll add it as a labelled row that runs off the edge on the next republish, so the yardstick order (persistence, then XGBoost, then us) is visible.

**"The encoder does not help" and the challenge.** It is a risk for the pitch, not for the brief. The brief asks to fine-tune a TSLM, compare it against baselines without leakage, and "explain the evidence and limitations"; a clean ablation is exactly that, and it agrees with OpenTSLM's own paper, where text input is competitive on short series and the encoder wins on long signals. Two ways to handle it, and I'd do both:
- Keep the encoder in the final model if the "text and encoder" run (scores due at ~00:55) is at least as good; then the submission is a genuine TSLM using the time-series path, and the ablation is a finding, not a confession.
- The one experiment that would let the encoder earn its place is to give it signals that cannot fit in a prompt: minute-resolution station and network lateness over 24 to 72 hours (thousands of points) instead of 72 hourly values. That is the "no context wall" argument from the brief. It needs a data-build change and a retrain, roughly two hours end to end. I'd start it only after the final safe run is submitted, if the night allows.

            "leak_minute": 1 - minute.sum(dim=-1),

        embeds, mask, _ = self._assemble(batch, [[] for _ in batch], left_pad=True)

content.subject: Probe data semantics across months
content.description: Check schema of Nov 2025 to Aug 2026 files, meaning of time / delay_in_min, run id from `id`, stop numbering.

content.subject: Build trip examples with leakage-safe features
content.description: DuckDB pipeline: runs, sampled (t0 stop, target stop) pairs, 4 series (run so far, fallback-key 30-day history, station 72h, network class 72h), text fields, tabular features, target minutes/cancelled, time split train/val/test. Smoke tests on synthetic data.

content.subject: Implement baselines and shared metrics
content.description: Persistence, key-history, XGBoost quantile + cancel classifier; metrics MAE of median, quantile CRPS, 10-90 coverage, P(late) Brier, cancel log loss, per lead bucket and class.

content.subject: Implement TSLM model, loss and readout
content.description: OpenTSLMSP subclass on unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B + m4-sp checkpoint: right padding, custom loss (CE on rationale, soft CE + CRPS at number token, hurdle cancel step), one-pass distribution readout, tests for token positions.

content.subject: Train and evaluate the TSLM on the devbox
content.description: Smoke train, then full run on the RTX 6000 Ada; evaluate on test with the shared metrics next to baselines; plain-CE ablation if time allows.

content.subject: Update DESIGN.md with implementation decisions and results
content.description: Rationale built from inputs only (never states the minute), loss only at the answer token, deviations found during implementation, results table.
content.activeForm: Recording results in DESIGN.md as runs finish

content.subject: Implement connection and journey probability
content.description: P(change works) from arriving and departing delay distributions, planned buffer and minimum transfer time; chained journey success; tests.

content.subject: Export trip examples as a TimeF dataset
content.description: TimeNet connector-style export of examples (four series, minute and cancellation tasks, metadata card) for the bonus points and dataset documentation.

content.subject: Forward test on live September data
content.description: Build examples from the raw September scrape (or Timetables API), predict before arrival, score once arrivals are published.

content.subject: Run ablations and text-only baseline on Nebius H100 jobs
content.description: Four one-GPU H100 jobs (2000 steps each): plain CE, text-only, ecg-sp start, random encoder; results in bucket runs/h100b-*; compare with compare_ablations.sh against baselines and the main run.

lastPrompt: And what is "CRPS" is that sth common or sth you made up?

content.text:
CRPS is standard, not ours. It stands for **Continuous Ranked Probability Score** and has been the default score for probabilistic forecasts since the 1970s; it is what weather services use to grade rain and temperature forecasts, and what the M5 and other forecasting competitions use for ranges. Gneiting and Raftery (2007, *Journal of the American Statistical Association*) is the standard reference; it is also in the OpenTSLM paper's world via every probabilistic forecasting benchmark.

What it measures: you predict a whole distribution ("30% chance of 0 min, 25% chance of 1 min, ..."), then the truth arrives, and CRPS is the area between your predicted cumulative curve and the step function of what happened. Two properties make it the right choice for us:

- **It is in the same unit as the target** (minutes here). If your forecast is a single point with no spread, CRPS equals the plain absolute error. So a CRPS of 2.9 minutes is directly comparable with a median error of 3.6 minutes: the range earns us about 0.7 minutes over guessing a point.
- **It is "proper"**: the only way to get the best possible score is to report your true beliefs. A model cannot game it by being vague (a wide range is punished) or by being overconfident (a narrow range that misses is punished harder).

We compute it from 19 quantiles of each forecast, which is the common approximation when a model produces quantiles, and the same code scores every model on the page, so the comparison is fair even if the absolute value has a small approximation error. I'll put a sentence with the name and the weather-forecasting origin into the glossary so a reader does not take it for a made-up number.

This is the integrator. Every other module has one job and a clean contract;
this one knows how all of them fit together, which is why it is not delegated.

Four things in TimeNet's contract will silently ruin a dataset if you get them
wrong, all verified against its source rather than its docs:

1. **``derive_schema`` aborts the build on any per-key inconsistency.** The
   descriptor is ``(key, annotation_type, value_type, unit, description)`` and
   two annotations sharing a key with any differing component raise. So
   ``value=3`` on one record and ``value=3.0`` on another kills the build; a key
   used span-less on one record and with a span on another kills the build. A
   key is one shape, forever. Hence ``_ANNOTATION_SPEC`` below: every key is
   declared once with its caster and its description, and nothing writes an
   annotation any other way.

2. **Auto-generated ids are UUIDv7** -- timestamped and random -- so a dataset

   is sorted before iteration. The framework hashes its outputs but never its
   inputs, and skips a rebuild purely on ``dataset_version`` existing, so
   reproducibility is entirely ours to enforce.

## 1. What db_route produces

A **different unit from ours**: one sample is `(service_group, station, anchor)` and the question is "over the 7 days *after* this anchor, how late will this train be at this stop" (entities.py:1-12, profiles.py:217). `service_group = train_type || ' -> ' || final_destination_station`, deliberately not line or train number (sources.py:44). Anchors are travel *dates*, 5 per entity, 35 days apart, hash-staggered, recency-weighted (anchors.py:1-56, :256).

Series: 6+4 named signals (profiles.py:36-51) computed as ratios of additive fact columns at three grains, station / line / pair (resample.py:94-170). Three layers: WEEK 168 x 1h, QUARTER 240 x 6h (60 d), SEASON 120 x 1d (profiles.py:124-165); profiles S/M/L/XM select subsets (profiles.py:195-212). Cap is OpenTSLM's 4096 samples (profiles.py:58), so hourly could in principle run 170 days. Every window ends at local midnight of the anchor (resample.py:228).

"Series families" are the five **cause families** `works, weather, technical, knock_on, staff` (causes.py:134), derived from IRIS `<m>` cause codes 1-69 with German texts (causes.py:34-112). "Causes" are per-stop codes; **disruption notices** are the dated `h`-type HIM messages with `valid_from/valid_to` (causes.py:237, :301). The "six regions" are munich/berlin/hamburg/cologne/frankfurt/stuttgart, each a station-name seed plus one hop along local operators only, unioned into the **catchment** as EVA numbers (facts.py:123-151); measured 2,691 stations, 19,436 qualifying pairs (commit f880d02).

Labels (labels.py:154): `departure_delay_min`, `arrival_delay_log1p`, `late_5min`, `late_5_share`, `dominant_cause_family`, family shares, plus ~20 leak-free `ctx_*` slots for the rationale (labels.py:109). Tasks are scalar / classification / answer-with-rationale, rendered to OpenTSLM's 5-key dict by bridge.py (bridge.py:24-30, :471, :673).

## 2. Sources and output

Same `piebro/deutsche-bahn-data` monthly parquet as ours (sources.py:15-19), **plus the `raw_data/` IRIS XML**, which is the only place cause codes and notice texts survive (causes.py:5-8, facts.py:97). No other API. Facts are three hourly parquets `hourly_station/line/pair` with sums and counts only, station set pinned to the top 400 present in every month (facts.py:63-83, :419, :530). Cause shards land in `/outputs/db_route/causes|notices/<eva-fingerprint>/<day>.parquet` on the mounted Nebius bucket (remote_extract.py:230-238, facts.py:252). **No bucket name or path is in the repo**; only `NEBIUS_OUTPUT_VOLUME` (a `storagebucket-...` resource id) in `app/backend/.env.example:30-33`.

## 3. Join keys

Entity key is `(service_group, station_name)` strings (resample.py:108); fact tables are keyed on `station_name`, not EVA (facts.py:530). EVA is used only to draw the catchment and filter raw XML. The one key that joins to us cleanly is the **per-stop-event id**: `causes.stop_id = events.id` (facts.py:487), the same `id` column of the processed monthly parquet. Time: hourly buckets on a global grid seeded at 2024-01-01 local (resample.py:81, :250), service day offset 3 h (sources.py:37).

## 4. Maturity

147 tests across 7 files, all cross-module imports resolve and every file parses; fixtures are real DuckDB tables with the true column names (tests/fixtures.py:1-14), so the suite is plausibly green given `duckdb`, `pyarrow`, `timenet`, `opentslm` (none installed in this checkout). entities.py, anchors.py, facts.py, bridge.py and validate.py all have CLIs. **build.py is the hole**: 316 lines of helpers (`caption_for`, `record_id_for`, `works_intervals`, `z_safe`, `_ANNOTATION_SPEC`), it imports the TimeNet task types but never uses them, has no `build_dataset`, no CLI and no test file (build.py:306 `__all__`). So nothing outside tests ever constructs a `TimeFDataset`, and there is no end-to-end run. validate.py checks source shape (monotonicity, duplicate stop ids, planned-vs-actual, the 2025-11-02 basis step), per-record series shape/length, imputed fraction, answer-matches-target, rationale numbers, phase alignment by cross-correlation, then cross-profile bundle-sha and split identity (validate.py:299-467, :584-902, :1047-1150).

Attach the **hourly station panel** as a long series. `FactCache.series(signal, layer, key, first)` (resample.py:451) takes an arbitrary integer bucket index, so with `Layer("week","1 hour", 720, ...)` and `first = bucket_index(t0_hour, 3600) - 720` you get a 30-day hourly `station_delay` / `station_cancel_rate` / `station_throughput` array plus a `present` mask ending at *our* `t0`, no midnight constraint (only `FactCache.window` forces midnight, resample.py:493).
